paragraph_text: \textbf{Theme 2: stable predictions do not guarantee stable explanations (RQ2).} The \mappe{} studies relating prediction-side quantities to explanation change agree the link is weak. Under attack, prediction robustness and explanation stability were distinct axes \cite{S59}; quantised models kept their ROC-AUC while SHAP rankings changed \cite{S50}; prediction-equivalent models from different hypothesis classes gave different attributions \cite{S75}; and better accuracy did not bring more reliable explanations \cite{S51,S79}. Only \mappp{} studies keep perturbations that leave the prediction unchanged \cite{S09,S25,S62}, and none in our extraction tests at the instance level whether the size of the prediction change predicts that of the explanation change.

paragraph_text: \textbf{Theme 3: instability has identifiable mechanisms (RQ3).} Instability is tied to a threshold or boundary in \mapmechthr{} studies \cite{S02,S19,S23,S25,S59,S75,S77}. Crossing a split in a single tree makes the Lipschitz ratio of random-forest SHAP diverge, which combining weak-learner explanations reduces \cite{S25}. XGBoost's piecewise-constant surface defeats gradient-free attacks yet leaves explanations unstable \cite{S59}; gradient-boosted trees show the same instability near segment boundaries as smooth non-linear models \cite{S77}. Explainer uncertainty grows with decision-boundary complexity \cite{S19} and falls with predictor smoothness \cite{S23}. For LIME, the random neighbourhood with its sample-size and proximity settings drives repeated-call variation \cite{S02,S08,S10}. Collinearity is the best-documented data mechanism (\mapmechcoll{} studies) \cite{S43,S53,S66,S75}: 68\% of 77 datasets showed SHAP instability, with rankings of correlated pairs close to a coin flip \cite{S43}. KernelSHAP adds Monte-Carlo error \cite{S18,S21,S31}, whereas TreeSHAP was near-deterministic \cite{S45,S46}. No study, however, counts how many split thresholds or bin edges a perturbation crosses.

paragraph_text: \textbf{Theme 4: predicting instability is possible but rarely cheap (RQ3).} \mapdiag{} studies attach an uncertainty or reliability estimate, for example Bayesian or bootstrap intervals \cite{S05,S11,S35}, distributional SHAP \cite{S73,S74}, model-set importance clouds \cite{S71} and tree-ensemble epistemic uncertainty \cite{S47}. Most need resampling or repeated calls, the cost a warning score should avoid. The revised map identifies \mapdiagfree{} perturbation-free predictors with different targets: epistemic uncertainty correlated strongly and negatively with stability \cite{S52}, instability was lower where forecast uncertainty was low \cite{S77}, a tree-structure score tracked disagreement between prediction-equivalent models \cite{S75}; and a split-count screen flagged ranking instability across retrained models \cite{S43}. paragraph_text: \textbf{How this changes the Assignment 1 problem.} The problem stays; its framing is sharpened. Novelty must be narrowed: prediction-preserving filters exist \cite{S09,S25,S62}; what is new is testing the prediction-to-explanation link for SHAP and LIME together on linear and tree-ensemble models against each explainer's noise floor. It should explain instability, not only measure it, by logging threshold and bin-edge crossings and controlling collinearity and class imbalance \cite{S29,S43,S53}. Finally, it should test whether a score computed from the trees alone can flag fragile explanations before any perturbation, with uncertainty-based scores \cite{S52,S77} as comparison. The revised statement reads: \textit{under prediction-preserving perturbations, does the size of a prediction change indicate the size of the SHAP or LIME explanation change for logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost beyond each explainer's own noise; is the change explained by split-threshold and bin-edge crossings; and can a score computed from the model alone predict it?}
